Watching this pageant clip, I couldnât help but ask myself, why do I see what Iâve experienced reflected in almost every interaction between women I come across online?

Not every woman standing beside you is rooting for you. 

Some will smile in your face, applaud your accomplishments, and call themselves your friend, but struggle to genuinely celebrate you when your light starts shining a little brighter than theirs.

And thatâs what gets me. 

Why does another woman winning have to feel like youâre losing? 

Why canât we celebrate each other, open doors for each other, share opportunities, and genuinely want to see each other succeed without comparison, competition, or hidden intentions?

Real sisterhood is more than words. Itâs how you show up for women when thereâs nothing to gain for yourself. 

Itâs celebrating them when theyâre in the room and speaking highly of them when theyâre not. 

Itâs making room at the table instead of trying to knock someone else out of their seat.

Another womanâs crown doesnât diminish yours. 

Her success doesnât take away from your own. 

There is room for all of us to grow, shine, and win.

Iâve experienced enough to know that everyone standing beside you isnât necessarily standing with you. 

Pay attention to who genuinely wants to see you rise and who is waiting for you to fall.

We need more women who understand that supporting another woman doesnât make you any less. 

It makes room for all of us to win. â¤ï¸

The Graduate (1967), directed by Mike Nichols from a screenplay by Buck Henry and Calder Willingham adapted from Charles Webbâs novel, follows Benjamin Braddock (Dustin Hoffman), a recent college graduate returning to his affluent Southern California home. Adrift and alienated, he is seduced by Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft), the wife of his fatherâs business partner, in an affair that begins as escape and quickly becomes a source of deeper confusion. When he meets and falls for her daughter Elaine (Katharine Ross), Benjaminâs passivity turns into desperate pursuit, culminating in the filmâs famous final sequence. The picture captures the restlessness of a young man pressured by parental expectations yet unable to articulate what he wants, set against the polished surfaces of suburban life and scored by Simon & Garfunkel songs that underscore his isolation.

Critically and commercially successful, the film became a defining portrait of generational friction in the late 1960s, blending sharp comedy with an undercurrent of melancholy. Hoffmanâs awkward, laconic performance and Bancroftâs poised, predatory Mrs. Robinson created iconic screen figures, while the storyâs frank treatment of sex, class, and aimlessness resonated with audiences questioning postwar conformity. Nominated for seven Academy Awards and winning Best Director for Nichols, *The Graduate* influenced subsequent American cinema in its visual style, editing, and willingness to leave its protagonistâs future unresolved. Its closing momentsâBenjamin and Elaine on the bus, their expressions shifting from triumph to uncertaintyâremain among the most discussed endings in film history, encapsulating the gap between rebellion and the difficulty of knowing what comes next.

ð GTA players have spent years accusing Los Santos traffic of deliberately swerving into them at the worst possible moment.

Clips like this are exactly why the theory has become such a long-running joke within the GTA community.

One popular explanation claimed Rockstar intentionally used traffic to slow players down at extreme speeds so the game world had more time to load, but former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij recently disputed that theory.

Vermeij explained that the sudden lane changes are random and can become especially abrupt when road-network nodes are positioned too close together.

He did confirm that GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas and GTA IV used certain zones with increased air resistance to limit player speed, just not by intentionally sending NPC cars into their path.

So while GTA traffic can absolutely feel like it has a personal vendetta against you, the chaos appears to be a side effect of how the traffic system behaves rather than a secret anti-speed mechanic.

label_values.value: This is the thing about Ai in gamedev: While I don't struggle with this issue anymore, when I was learning some bugs held me up FOR WEEKS. Not days, 2, 3, 4, 5 weeks. And good luck hiring someone to fix your extremely niche problem in a giant nooby-sphagetti coded project (trust me, I tried). That said, I am not all for all-coded games. However, getting a little help here and there, especially if it's just a bug or explanation of systems and etc does not bother me at all. This is the thing: If you google the question, chances are Google Ai summary will have the answer right there. You'd have to physically not look at that, and dive into some forums which may or may not have an answer to your system (usually, they don't). I was blessed enough to work in an engine where there was a wonderful community that helped people with small issues like this, and there was almost always a few people online that could help. I spent countless hours there when I was learning. The thing is, the more advanced I and my code got, the less people there was available to help me, and the other thing, most engines don't have a community like that. Anyway: what's your take on this whole situation?

In September, Jacob Coxon, along with other AI security researchers made headlines for quitting Anthropic. He tweeted that âthe people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.â This week, at a talk hosted by Stanford University, Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, defended keeping his AI stock, saying âI like money bro.â

âIf I thought for a moment that donating it like would change anything then sure, Iâd do it,â Coxon told political science professor Robert Reich who then pushed him further about how giving it away would give him âmoral credibility.â Coxon then responded to Reich saying, âI agree but you could also stop asking the question.â Alex Kantrowitz of Big Tech shared a clip of the exchange on X.

A man believed to be K-pop boy group RIIZEâs manager has drawn criticism after footage showed him pushing a woman into an airport fixture at South Koreaâs Incheon International Airport on Nov. 18.

According to Yonhap News Agency, the group was passing through Terminal 2âs duty-free area en route to New York.

Access to the area is limited to passengers with valid tickets and airport personnel, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

Some fans were believed to have booked flights scheduled around the groupâs departure, although it remains unconfirmed whether they actually flew.

The footage divided opinion online, with criticism directed at both the use of force and fans crowding around the group.

Police have received no reports of the incident and are not investigating it, according to Yonhap.

The incident has renewed concerns over celebrity security at Incheon Airport, where crowds have previously disrupted passengers and prompted complaints about excessive force.

The other sailor appears to evade the attempted strike and respond with a series of punches, bringing the confrontation to a quick end.

The identities of those involved, the circumstances leading up to the altercation, and whether any disciplinary action followed have not been independently verified. The footage alone does not establish the full context of the incident.

Military barracks are expected to maintain standards of discipline and safety, and physical confrontations can carry serious consequences even when one person appears to act in self-defence.

Question for the public: How should military authorities distinguish legitimate self-defence from excessive force when investigating a barracks fight?

I wish I had some kinda guidance before I started travelling ð¤

I have always really avoided conflict, and so learning how to protect myself and set boundaries travelling - has been a huge journey for me 

Itâs so easy to want to diffuse a situation by just excusing itâ¦
âOh heâs just acting like that because weâre culturally differentâ 
Or
âheâs not meaning to make me uncomfortable â

For me it was making the decision - I KNOW what I am comfortable with. That does not adjust with my environment.
You do not need to adapt your boundaries for a scenario, or a manâs cultural differencesâ¦
If something makes you uncomfortable then it makes you uncomfortable 

Setting boundaries is genuinely a skill and takes practice! Especially when you are young and new to travelling

What I did which really helped, was come up with simple responses - to clearly display my boundaries in any situation.

Having these ready in my head, made knowing what my âtrue selfâ would want me to say - much easier, and it prevented me from making excuses for them to avoid conflict in the moment. 

With time it gets easier and less uncomfortable! 

The internet makes it seem like you should go travelling and live like youâre in a movie. This is your reminder that you should be aware always be aware and take precautions, so that you can have the BEST travel experiences possible and gain that worldly knowledge ð¥°

Trans bus driver fired for wearing a skimpy schoolgirl outfit on the kidsâ âLolita Lineâ route is now suing the school district for discrimination.

In 2025, driver L.Z. was filmed outside a York Catholic elementary school in Vaughan, Ontario, wearing a short pink skirt, frilly white top, and knee-high stockings while transporting children. A handwritten sign on the bus read âLolita Line.â 

Parents raised concerns and the third-party operator removed the driver from the route. L.Z., who identifies as a transgender woman, later filed a human rights complaint against the school board and bus company alleging discrimination on the basis of gender identity, sex, and ethnic origin. 

The name âLolitaâ comes from Vladimir Nabokovâs novel about an adult manâs fixation on a 12-year-old girl and was also the informal nickname given to Jeffrey Epsteinâs private jet.

A teenage English boxer says he was left "broken" after he was banned from competing at the Under-19 World Championships because his team forgot to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.
 
George Francis, 18, was due to fight in the 60kg category in Budva, Montenegro last month.
 
But he says that he was informed he was ineligible only hours before the draw because of an "administrative oversight" by governing body England Boxing.
 
"They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically," Francis told BBC Sport.
 
"The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.
 
"Somehow I wasn't on the system. Apparently, there were no qualified doctors in Budva to do it. It's crazy."
 
A multiple schoolboy and junior national champion, Francis said he had been training "non-stop" for the "dream" of representing England in his first World Championships.

One thing I was intentional about throughout my premed journey was pursuing experiences that genuinely interested me, NOT just things I thought would impress an admissions committee.

Yes, you need clinical experience, volunteering, leadership, shadowing, and research. Those are the overarching categories to consider.

But what you do WITHIN those categories is where your individuality can shine. ð

Ask yourself:

â¡ï¸ What communities do I want to serve?

â¡ï¸ Am I interested in public health, research, business, or something else?

â¡ï¸ Are there specific patient populations Iâm passionate about, such as children, older adults, or underserved communities?

You donât have to wait until medical school to start exploring these interests!

And PLEASE donât feel pressured to have a perfectly crafted âthemeâ throughout your application.

If you looked at mine, youâd see experiences across several different areas that donât necessarily fit into one neat box.

YOU ARE NOT ONE-DIMENSIONAL!

Youâre more than your GPA, MCAT, clinical hours, or research experiences.

Your application should reflect your passions, interests, personality, and preparation for medicine, not some imaginary version of the perfect applicant.

Build an application that shows admissions committees WHO YOU ARE, not just what youâve accomplished.

Harvard admitted them. Then Harvard saw the group chat.

In 2017, at least ten admitted students had their Harvard offers taken back after screenshots from a private group chat reached the school. The students thought the chat was private. It wasnât.

And it isnât just Harvard. In Kaplanâs 2023 survey, 67% of admissions officers said an applicantâs social media is fair game, and 28% said they have actually gone and looked at a studentâs profile. The ones who look say they find something that hurts more often than something that helps.

A private account is not the protection most families think it is. The profile photo, the bio, the tagged pictures, and your studentâs comments on other peopleâs posts are all still visible, and a screenshot can travel anywhere.

Tonight, take two minutes and search your studentâs name the way a stranger would. If you can find it, so can they.

Follow @eaglecollegeadvising for the parts of this process colleges do not explain.

Sources: Kaplan admissions officer survey, 2023; Harvard Crimson, 2017.

CCTV footage from an internet cafÃ© in Ya'an, Sichuan province, China, has gone viral on social media, drawing widespread praise for the establishment's owner after an accidental equipment collapse. In the video, a cleaning worker finishing her shift in an empty section of the cafÃ© pushed a gaming chair back toward a long computer desk, inadvertently bumping it and causing the entire row of five desktop computers, monitors, and accessories to crash to the floor.

Visibly shaken by the incident, the worker immediately reported the accident to management and offered to take financial responsibility for the damages, which were estimated at around 10,000 yuan (approximately $1,500). However, instead of demanding compensation, the cafÃ© owner reviewed the security camera footage and determined that the long desk had not been properly anchored or securely installed.

Refusing to accept any payment from the employee, the owner absorbed the full repair costs himself and thanked the worker for inadvertently exposing a serious structural hazard that could have injured patrons had the seats been occupied. Following the incident, management arranged for technicians to reinforce all computer tables across the venue, earning widespread commendation online for prioritizing workplace fairness and customer safety over financial recovery.

Two years later, theyâll be applying as a transfer student, and the money on the table may look different.

Parents, yâall gotta be careful with that blanket advice. What if the school you crossed off the list wouldâve offered your child a full ride? ð

Real sisterhood is more than words. Itâs how you show up for women when thereâs nothing to gain for yourself. 

Itâs celebrating them when theyâre in the room and speaking highly of them when theyâre not. 

Itâs making room at the table instead of trying to knock someone else out of their seat.

Another womanâs crown doesnât diminish yours. 

Her success doesnât take away from your own. 

There is room for all of us to grow, shine, and win.

Iâve experienced enough to know that everyone standing beside you isnât necessarily standing with you. 

Pay attention to who genuinely wants to see you rise and who is waiting for you to fall.

The Graduate (1967), directed by Mike Nichols from a screenplay by Buck Henry and Calder Willingham adapted from Charles Webbâs novel, follows Benjamin Braddock (Dustin Hoffman), a recent college graduate returning to his affluent Southern California home. Adrift and alienated, he is seduced by Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft), the wife of his fatherâs business partner, in an affair that begins as escape and quickly becomes a source of deeper confusion. When he meets and falls for her daughter Elaine (Katharine Ross), Benjaminâs passivity turns into desperate pursuit, culminating in the filmâs famous final sequence. The picture captures the restlessness of a young man pressured by parental expectations yet unable to articulate what he wants, set against the polished surfaces of suburban life and scored by Simon & Garfunkel songs that underscore his isolation.

Critically and commercially successful, the film became a defining portrait of generational friction in the late 1960s, blending sharp comedy with an undercurrent of melancholy. Hoffmanâs awkward, laconic performance and Bancroftâs poised, predatory Mrs. Robinson created iconic screen figures, while the storyâs frank treatment of sex, class, and aimlessness resonated with audiences questioning postwar conformity. Nominated for seven Academy Awards and winning Best Director for Nichols, *The Graduate* influenced subsequent American cinema in its visual style, editing, and willingness to leave its protagonistâs future unresolved. Its closing momentsâBenjamin and Elaine on the bus, their expressions shifting from triumph to uncertaintyâremain among the most discussed endings in film history, encapsulating the gap between rebellion and the difficulty of knowing what comes next.

ð GTA players have spent years accusing Los Santos traffic of deliberately swerving into them at the worst possible moment.

Clips like this are exactly why the theory has become such a long-running joke within the GTA community.

One popular explanation claimed Rockstar intentionally used traffic to slow players down at extreme speeds so the game world had more time to load, but former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij recently disputed that theory.

Vermeij explained that the sudden lane changes are random and can become especially abrupt when road-network nodes are positioned too close together.

He did confirm that GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas and GTA IV used certain zones with increased air resistance to limit player speed, just not by intentionally sending NPC cars into their path.

So while GTA traffic can absolutely feel like it has a personal vendetta against you, the chaos appears to be a side effect of how the traffic system behaves rather than a secret anti-speed mechanic.

Do you think GTA VI needs smarter and more predictable traffic AI?

label_values.value: This is the thing about Ai in gamedev: While I don't struggle with this issue anymore, when I was learning some bugs held me up FOR WEEKS. Not days, 2, 3, 4, 5 weeks. However, getting a little help here and there, especially if it's just a bug or explanation of systems and etc does not bother me at all. This is the thing: If you google the question, chances are Google Ai summary will have the answer right there. You'd have to physically not look at that, and dive into some forums which may or may not have an answer to your system (usually, they don't). I was blessed enough to work in an engine where there was a wonderful community that helped people with small issues like this, and there was almost always a few people online that could help. I spent countless hours there when I was learning. The thing is, the more advanced I and my code got, the less people there was available to help me, and the other thing, most engines don't have a community like that. Anyway: what's your take on this whole situation?

âYou either crashed your A-levels or went to private school.â

Thatâs what a managing director replied after I emailed his firm looking for an opportunity.

I was a clueless first year sending emails to companies, and Iâd clearly caught an executive on a bad day. But once the sting wore off, his reply was the most useful feedback Iâd had, because it showed me exactly what Iâd got wrong.

â¢ Iâd emailed the CFO, whereas the COO was the person who owned hiring for that kind of role.

â¢ I referenced a deal that was six months old, because my outreach system was clumsy, and I now teach clients to find the most up to date information they can.

â¢ Their whole edge was frontier markets and I didnât mention it once, and relevance is the difference between a reply and getting binned.

â¢ Iâd asked for the wrong thing, using a word for a position the firm had never hired for, so now I say contribute or support.

â¢ Iâd left my A-levels off my CV, three Bs, and everything you include or leave out still signals something to an employer.

Would I work there now? No. But Iâm glad he replied the way he did, because the method he mocked, cold outreach from a nobody, is the one I used to land 15 offers that year.

Comment âOFFERâ and Iâll show you how I used his feedback to get those 15 offers myself, and how I can get you the finance offer you want in the next 28 days.

#email #outreach #career #graduate #finance

(thank you in advance to those who read this caption fully ð¤)

Rejection is hard to talk about.

But in a season where so many are celebrating med school interviews, residency interviews, acceptances, and exciting news, I know there are also people silently struggling with rejection right now.

I hope this brings you hope.

In college, I applied to an early med program that wouldâve let me go to med school without the MCAT or physics: the VERY two things I truly didnât believe I was capable of.

I never felt like I was strong enough for medicine, so this program felt like my ONE shot - a way in without having to face the doubts I carried so deeply.

Out of thousands of applicants, I was selected for an interview. My hopes skyrocketed. I prepared OBSESSIVELY and gave it everything I had.

And then I was rejected.

I was devastated.

What I couldnât see then, but understand now, is that this rejection wasnât a failure. It was a redirection.

That program wouldâve taken me far from home and family, far from a life I didnât yet realize I deeply wanted. I was willing to give up everything to become a doctor, but God knew my heart better than I did.

God was asking me to trust Him - to believe He would walk with me through the uncertainty, and that even closed doors could be part of a plan meant âto prosper and not to harm, to give hope and a future.â Jeremiah 29:11.

Two years later, I ended up exactly where I was meant to be - at the med school I attend now, close to home.

And now Iâm applying to residency, once again in a season of interviews, waiting, and trusting God with doors I canât control.

Funny how life brings you back to the same lessons in different seasons :â)

I share this for three reasons:

1. to be transparent about failure on a platform that too often highlights only the best versions of ourselves

2. to share a piece of my testimony

3. to honor the blessing of a mom who sat with me in the pain and reminded me of Godâs truth when I couldnât see it myself through the tears

maybe someone else needs the reminder today: rejection can be a redirection - one step closer to understanding Godâs plan ð¤

#FaithInMedicine

âIf I thought for a moment that donating it like would change anything then sure, Iâd do it,â Coxon told political science professor Robert Reich who then pushed him further about how giving it away would give him âmoral credibility.â Coxon then responded to Reich saying, âI agree but you could also stop asking the question.â Alex Kantrowitz of Big Tech shared a clip of the exchange on X. 

Further in the conversation posted in length on the Stanford HAI YouTube channel, Coxon also questions if his decision to leave the industry was the right one, and said it was possible that he could go back.

I wish I had some kinda guidance before I started travelling ð¤

I have always really avoided conflict, and so learning how to protect myself and set boundaries travelling - has been a huge journey for me 

Itâs so easy to want to diffuse a situation by just excusing itâ¦
âOh heâs just acting like that because weâre culturally differentâ 
Or
âheâs not meaning to make me uncomfortable â

For me it was making the decision - I KNOW what I am comfortable with. That does not adjust with my environment.
You do not need to adapt your boundaries for a scenario, or a manâs cultural differencesâ¦
If something makes you uncomfortable then it makes you uncomfortable 

Setting boundaries is genuinely a skill and takes practice! Especially when you are young and new to travelling

What I did which really helped, was come up with simple responses - to clearly display my boundaries in any situation.

Having these ready in my head, made knowing what my âtrue selfâ would want me to say - much easier, and it prevented me from making excuses for them to avoid conflict in the moment. 

With time it gets easier and less uncomfortable! 

The internet makes it seem like you should go travelling and live like youâre in a movie. This is your reminder that you should be aware always be aware and take precautions, so that you can have the BEST travel experiences possible and gain that worldly knowledge ð¥°

A routine shopping trip turned into an ugly confrontation at a Walmart in Moreno Valley, California, after a Black customer accused an employee of racial profiling and making derogatory remarks. #racialprofiling #fypreelsã·ãviralã· #shoppingwhileblack #racialjustice #walmart 

According to the customer, the confrontation began when an employee asked to check his receipt.  The situation allegedly escalated when the worker began removing merchandise from his shopping cart and made a racially charged remark suggesting that people like him are always trying to steal.

LET THAT SINK IN.

A Black man walks into a store to spend his hard-earned money, and instead of being treated like a valued customer, he says he was treated like a criminal.

Checking receipts may be store policy, but racial insults, humiliation, and discriminatory treatment should NEVER be part of anyoneâs job description.

And hereâs what makes this particularly disturbing:  Weâre in 2026, and Black Americans are STILL having to defend their right to simply exist in public spaces without being stereotyped, suspected, or disrespected.

Racism doesnât become acceptable just because someone is wearing a company uniform.

The employee deserves a fair investigation, and the customer deserves to have his allegations taken seriously.  Accountability matters.

At what point does a routine receipt check cross the line into racial profiling?

Should employees who make racist remarks toward customers be immediately terminated?

Better stories.  Bigger conversations.

A teenage English boxer says he was left "broken" after he was banned from competing at the Under-19 World Championships because his team forgot to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.
 
George Francis, 18, was due to fight in the 60kg category in Budva, Montenegro last month.
 
But he says that he was informed he was ineligible only hours before the draw because of an "administrative oversight" by governing body England Boxing.
 
"They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically," Francis told BBC Sport.
 
"The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.
 
"Somehow I wasn't on the system. Apparently, there were no qualified doctors in Budva to do it. It's crazy."
 
A multiple schoolboy and junior national champion, Francis said he had been training "non-stop" for the "dream" of representing England in his first World Championships.

Afraid of not getting into medical school? â¹ï¸â¬ï¸

Follow @journey.with.jayden and Iâll show you how to build an AUTHENTIC application that you can feel confident about.

One thing I was intentional about throughout my premed journey was pursuing experiences that genuinely interested me, NOT just things I thought would impress an admissions committee.

Yes, you need clinical experience, volunteering, leadership, shadowing, and research. Those are the overarching categories to consider.

But what you do WITHIN those categories is where your individuality can shine. ð

Ask yourself:

â¡ï¸ What communities do I want to serve?

â¡ï¸ Am I interested in public health, research, business, or something else?

â¡ï¸ Are there specific patient populations Iâm passionate about, such as children, older adults, or underserved communities?

You donât have to wait until medical school to start exploring these interests!

And PLEASE donât feel pressured to have a perfectly crafted âthemeâ throughout your application.

If you looked at mine, youâd see experiences across several different areas that donât necessarily fit into one neat box.

YOU ARE NOT ONE-DIMENSIONAL!

Youâre more than your GPA, MCAT, clinical hours, or research experiences.

Your application should reflect your passions, interests, personality, and preparation for medicine, not some imaginary version of the perfect applicant.

Build an application that shows admissions committees WHO YOU ARE, not just what youâve accomplished.

And if youâre struggling to figure out how to do that, my DMs are ALWAYS open! â¤ï¸

Harvard admitted them. Then Harvard saw the group chat.

In 2017, at least ten admitted students had their Harvard offers taken back after screenshots from a private group chat reached the school. The students thought the chat was private. It wasnât.

And it isnât just Harvard. In Kaplanâs 2023 survey, 67% of admissions officers said an applicantâs social media is fair game, and 28% said they have actually gone and looked at a studentâs profile. The ones who look say they find something that hurts more often than something that helps.

A private account is not the protection most families think it is. The profile photo, the bio, the tagged pictures, and your studentâs comments on other peopleâs posts are all still visible, and a screenshot can travel anywhere.

Tonight, take two minutes and search your studentâs name the way a stranger would. If you can find it, so can they.

Follow @eaglecollegeadvising for the parts of this process colleges do not explain.

Sources: Kaplan admissions officer survey, 2023; Harvard Crimson, 2017.
